Start on Casual. Go CT and take the M4A1-S as soon as possible. Crouch always, never fire more than four shots at a time. Aim for center mass until you're comfortable shooting.

TheWarOwl on YouTube is a great resource, and a lot of his matchmaking academy videos and analyses of pro matches are good to watch. Many pro players have done tutorials, that's always worth looking at.

But, I think that the biggest thing is your frame of mind when playing the game. For me, Id' say that CS:GO is a FPS experience like nothing else I'd ever played, and that it requires a different mindset. The best thing that you can do for yourself is to keep calm.

If I were to make a list of things I'd tell myself to do if I was brand new again, it'd be this:

  • Spend some time watching videos

  • Find game settings that work for you. (mouse sensitivity is important, as is the dpi of your mouse. most people recommend 2.0 sens @ 400 dpi. I play at 1.25 sens on 800 dpi.)

  • Deathmatch, deathmatch, deathmatch. DM is a great way to practice your aim. Crosshair placement is very important in this game, and it can be a really good/kind of fun experience to just throw some music on and focus on keeping your crosshair at head level.

  • Crosshair replacement is worth watching a video about, but in very dumbed down terms, you should always keep your crosshair at head level, and be aiming it where you think your enemy is going to be. adreN has a nice tutorial about this.

  • Community servers are a good alternative, and probably even preferable to valve DM servers, as you'll encounter generally more skilled competition, though valve DM would probably be good for a beginner.

  • Set up a crosshair that you like. Find out whether you'd rather have static or dynamic, classic or default, etc. There's a workshop map called "Crashz' Crosshair Generator v2" where you can look at different crosshairs on the wall, test them out against various background, and all you have to do is shoot the crosshair to keep it yours.

  • Another fun thing I like to do for aim practice is another workshop map called training_aim_csgo 2, which is a map where there's a big screen in front of you that targets appear on, and you just try to shoot each target before it disappears. There are 4 different levels, and on each different level you're further away, higher up, and the targets appear faster (I think.)

  • Make sure you're getting 60fps, preferably. CS:GO isn't too hard of a game to run, but I'm just saying that generally, it's worth it to drop visual settings to keep a steady 60.

  • HAVE AND USE A MICROPHONE. I'm not sure how I made it this far into this list without thinking about it, but I would definitely say that effective CS:GO competitive play requires teamwork and communication, and while you might not always get that from your teammates in matchmaking, it's important that you have it. Good communication and calling can save rounds/games. Don't be shy to use your microphone, either. Even if nobody else on your team is talking, make calls.

  • Stay positive. Everybody has a bad game once in a while, where they perform much worse than usual. These things happen. Remain calm and play your hardest. Some dude on the bottom of your team 0-18? Don't be yelling at him and criticizing him, it'll just make him play even worse, if anything. *Toxic, angry teammates? * Don't let them get to you. If your team is just angry and annoying, sometimes it may be worth losing the information from them to mute them, though Id' recommend just ignoring the bad/toxic stuff they say and just listening for info, unless they're playing loud music over VOIP or something like that.

  • Speaking of which, good calling. This is something that I find frustrating in most of my games, and feel a need to express/rant about here: There are different sections of every map, and they have call-out names. In CS:GO, these appear in the top left corner if you don't know them, and I wouldn't call it mandatory to know them all to start playing, as you'll pick them up over time.

Let's say you're on the dust2 map, playing as a counter-terrorist. At the start of the round, two of your teammates go to B-Site, one watches mid, one plays on catwalk, and you're the guy playing long. If you get flashbanged, don't say "they're long." say "flashes long" or "flashed long". If two people rush you and you die, say "two long." if one has an AWP (sniper rifle), note that. My biggest pet peeve right now is when somebody gets pushed by one person and says "oh they're long they're long", because unless you've literally seen all five people you can't make that call. Always call numbers. "3 long" "2 cat, 1 a site" "one pushing mid doors now", stuff like that.

  • The guns in CS:GO have recoil, and they have recoil patterns. It would do you very well to learn the recoil patterns of the AK-47, and the M4A4/ M4A1-S depending on which one you think you'll use. A4/A1-S is a different debate entirely, and one I won't get into.

  • Learn to accept that you're probably going to get beat. This is a hard one for me still, but I honestly have something close to a 50% winrate, since I solo q a lot and am not good enough to carry teams. You're going to encounter challenges, but the best thing you can do when getting out-played or beaten is to try and out-think your enemy, remain calm, and if you just can't beat them, then learn from them. Once you start playing competitive, your matches will automatically be saved for you for a while, and you can choose to download them, watch them, and play them back from the perspective of any participant in the match. Did you get rekt by some guy carrying the other team, dropping 30 kills? watch how he played. Watch yourself, see what you did wrong and could have done better.

If you actually own CS:GO, have a mic, and would like to learn a little bit, I wouldn't mind showing you some basic stuff in-game, though I'm not by any means the best source of knowledge out there. I'm USA-West Coast so pacific timezone, and I'm generally available after 2PM or so most days other than the weekends. Shoot me a PM and I'll add you on steam or something.

For reference, I have 402 hours played and 178 competitive wins, and I'm currently in the Gold Nova Master skill group. There are SO many things I myself still need to learn to improve, but I'm pretty capable of teaching basic, basic stuff.
